P2.strengths: Best balance on the first screen at both widths. It shows the title, outlet and date, the one-sentence framing (districts that might flip, progressives challenging Democrats), a two-row table of seats up and current splits, filter pills with counts, and the first seat cards, so a newcomer sees what this is and starts reading races without scrolling. Seat cards are named for a person ('Timm Ormsby's seat', 'Open: Rep. Timm Ormsby is retiring'), carry plain tags and party-count chips, and link related races to each other (Mena's Senate bid to her open House seat, Ryu to Salomon, Valdez to Krishnadasan). The filter explains its own criterion ('Seats in the 5th ... and 26th ... and the 42nd's Senate seat'). Fidelity is the most careful of the four: it flags the article's 29-20 vs 30-19 Senate inconsistency, says 'The article names no other candidates for this seat' on Conway's seat, marks Gary Parker's party as not stated, and keeps verbatim source sentences per race.
P2.weaknesses: Every candidate sits behind a click, and several one-line facts sit behind a second, nested click ('Civic work ▾', 'Earlier work ▾', 'Income tax vote ▾'). That is disclosure inside disclosure for single sentences. Collapsed text is display:none, so browser find cannot locate a candidate such as Joe Bushnell until the right card is opened. Open status is said three times per card (title, status line, 'Open seat' tag). The calendar and the primary and general dates sit at the very bottom, not up top.
P2.regions: Header with chamber table; filter pills and their explanation line; district headers with lean notes; collapsed seat cards (chamber chip, status, tags, party counts, 'N candidates ▾'); expanded 'The seat' and 'The field', including the 42nd's 'Senate math' note and the 26th's cross-race links; 'Source sentences' details; bottom 'The 2026 election' calendar and aims; phone view of the 5th expanded.

Z2.strengths: A master-detail layout that suits a dozen seats. The left list is grouped by district, with area and lean ('Spokane · Reliably Democratic', 'One of the few ... battleground'), and each row names the seat holder and their status ('Steve Conway · retiring', 'Sharlett Mena (D) · running for the Senate', 'incumbent') plus a party mix. A newcomer can read the list as a summary. The detail pane opens on a full race at once: a Leaving or Incumbent line, the district, seat facts, and a candidate table with Background and Backed by columns, all without nested disclosure. Linked races jump correctly ('Her House seat, now open →'). Verbatim article paragraphs are tucked away per race. The header strip carries splits and both election dates.
Z2.weaknesses: There is no framing sentence on screen. The article's point (flip targets and progressive challenges) is hidden in the 'cycle & source' dialog. 'Mark' only highlights rows and never filters, and it opens with 'Might flip' preselected, so the purple bars on some rows read as selection or importance without explanation. The tag criteria are never defined. Creydt's bullet repeats the article's '29-20 majority' while the header says 30-19, with no note. The phone view gives the list 40% of the height and leaves the detail cramped below it. The full-screen slideshow is a generic app device this content does not need.
Z2.regions: Header strip and 'cycle & source' dialog; Mark row (switched to Own-party challenge); grouped district list scrolled to the 29th/32nd/42nd; detail cards for Conway, Mena and Shewmake with the candidate/background/backed-by table; go-links between Conway and Mena; 'Article text for this race' expander; Full screen deck; phone view of Ryu's seat.

R9.strengths: The clearest explanation for someone who knows nothing. It has the full headline and dek, a 'What's at stake' paragraph, red/blue majority bars, and a four-step calendar (filing, Aug. 4 top-two primary, Nov. 3, January). Each race card leads with a newsy headline that tells the story ('Rep. Cindy Ryu challenges Sen. Jesse Salomon', 'Appointed Rep. Zach Hall, D-Issaquah, faces three challengers'), then gives a short summary and every candidate inline. Nothing is hidden, so browser find works for any name. A legend defines each tag, including what 'Could flip' means. Jump-to-district links and a sticky filter with a chamber toggle make the long page navigable. A footer notes the 29-20 vs 30-19 discrepancy.
R9.weaknesses: On desktop the first screen holds no races at all, and on the phone it holds only the title and dek. The races start about 1,140px down on desktop and 1,820px down on the phone, and the page runs 9,000 to 12,000px. Every D pill also carries the word 'Democrat' beneath it. The 26th's 2025 contest is told in both the district intro and the race summary. Conway's open Senate seat is folded into Mena's House card instead of standing as its own race. The Senate filter and the open-seat count (5) therefore miss an open Senate seat the article names, and Mena never appears as a Senate candidate.
R9.regions: Hero header; 'What's at stake' bars and calendar; tag legend; jump-to-district nav (tested on the 32nd); sticky filter and chamber toggle (Could flip + Senate gave 2); 32nd and 26th race cards on desktop and phone; footer note.

R5.strengths: Compact and fast to scan. All 13 seats fit in one flat list on desktop, with district, chamber, race type and a chip per candidate. A Race filter works, and one click (or the arrow keys) brings up a clean detail panel with labelled facts (Seat, Last race, Area, Lean) and candidate cards showing role, notes and backers, all visible without further clicks. The info dialog gathers the statewide context and the source well. Party for Gary Parker is marked as not stated.
R5.weaknesses: It is the most cryptic for a newcomer. Seats are labelled by bare surname ('Ormsby', 'Hall', 'Conway'), with no first names and no 'retiring' or 'running for Senate' status in the list. The field is shown as strings of D/R/N letter chips. A second 'Mark' row (Incumbents / Democrats / Republicans / No party) recolors those chips with no explanation. There is no framing sentence on screen, and the header is a monospace stat strip. The list has no district context or grouping, the tag criteria are undefined, and there is no source text. The phone view squeezes the detail below a 40% list. Conway's seat shows only Mena, with no note that the article names no one else.
R5.regions: Header stat strip; Race and Mark chip rows (tested Might flip and Republicans); flat district/seat/field list; detail panel for Ormsby, Conway and Mena; info dialog; full-screen deck; phone view of Salomon's seat.

summary: P2 was the only page whose first screen gave a newcomer both the article's framing and the races themselves. Its seat cards named who is leaving or running, its filters explained their criteria, and it was the most careful about what the article does and does not say. Z2 and R5 offered quicker lookup through a list and detail panel, but they dropped the framing sentence, and R5's surname-and-letter-chip list is hard to read cold. R9 explained the most but pushed every race below the first screen and folded one open Senate seat into another race.
